blocks.text: ZeRO-3 completes the progression started in ZeRO-1 and ZeRO-2, additionally sharding the model weights themselves across devices, so that no single device ever needs to hold the complete model, gradients, and optimizer state all at once, delivering the maximum memory savings within the ZeRO family at the cost of the highest communication overhead.

This closing topic of the Distributed Training Techniques module compares ZeRO-3 directly against model parallelism, covered earlier, and against combining it with PEFT methods, tying together the full sharding picture built across this module.
1. What ZeRO Stage 3 Adds

blocks.alt: ZeRO-2 shards optimizer state and gradients, ZeRO-3 adds sharding model weights too

blocks.text: ZeRO-3 takes the sharding covered in ZeRO-1 and ZeRO-2, optimizer state and gradients, and extends it one step further, sharding the model weights themselves, meaning every one of the four main training components, weights, gradients, optimizer state, and activations, addressed separately through gradient checkpointing, gets handled efficiently.
2. Sharding Model Parameters Themselves

blocks.alt: Optimizer state, gradients, and now model weights are all sharded together under ZeRO-3

blocks.text: With model weights sharded, this stage closely resembles the FSDP approach covered earlier in this module, gathering the full weights only temporarily when a specific computation needs them, then discarding the gathered copy again, since ZeRO-3 and FSDP share very similar underlying ideas.

code.content:
# A conceptual sketch, ZeRO-3 shards all three components
device_optimizer_shard = optimizer_state[device_rank::num_devices]
device_gradient_shard = gradients[device_rank::num_devices]
device_weight_shard = model_weights[device_rank::num_devices]
# Full weights gathered only temporarily when a layer needs them

blocks.text: 3. ZeRO-3's Maximum Memory Savings

blocks.alt: ZeRO-2 savings are compared against the maximum savings ZeRO-3 delivers

blocks.text: Because ZeRO-3 shards all three major components, it delivers the largest memory reduction within the ZeRO family, letting significantly larger models be trained on the same set of devices compared to ZeRO-1 or ZeRO-2 alone, which still require full model weights on every device.

blocks.text: 4. The Communication Cost of ZeRO-3

blocks.alt: Every forward and backward step gathers weight shards, producing the highest communication cost

blocks.text: This maximum memory savings comes at a real cost, since weights are no longer replicated, they must be gathered from across devices for essentially every layer computation during both the forward and backward pass, making ZeRO-3 the most communication intensive of the three stages, echoing the gather and discard pattern covered in the FSDP topic.

blocks.title: This tradeoff mirrors the tensor parallelism versus pipeline parallelism comparison earlier in this module
blocks.content: Just as tensor parallelism finer grained splitting required more frequent communication than pipeline parallelism coarser staging, ZeRO-3 finer grained weight sharding requires more frequent communication than ZeRO-1 or ZeRO-2.

blocks.text: 5. ZeRO-3 and Very Large Models

blocks.alt: A model that does not fit even with ZeRO-2 makes ZeRO-3 necessary

blocks.text: ZeRO-3 becomes necessary specifically when a model is large enough that even sharding optimizer state and gradients under ZeRO-2 still leaves the fully replicated model weights themselves too large to fit on the available devices, exactly the scenario the earlier Model Parallelism topic also addressed.
6. ZeRO-3 vs Model Parallelism

blocks.alt: ZeRO-3 uses the same model on every shard while model parallelism assigns different model portions to different devices

blocks.text: ZeRO-3 and model parallelism, covered earlier in this module, both address fitting a model too large for one device, but through different mechanisms, ZeRO-3 treats every device as logically running the same complete model, temporarily gathering full weights as needed, while model parallelism permanently assigns different portions of the model to different devices.
7. ZeRO-3's Practical Tradeoffs

Choosing ZeRO-3 means accepting its higher communication overhead in exchange for its maximum memory savings, a worthwhile tradeoff specifically when a model genuinely needs that level of memory reduction, but potentially unnecessary complexity if ZeRO-1 or ZeRO-2 alone would have sufficed for a smaller model.
8. Choosing Among ZeRO Stages

A practical approach starts with ZeRO-1, moving up to ZeRO-2 and then ZeRO-3 only as needed, checking at each step whether the additional memory savings from the next stage are actually necessary for a specific model and hardware combination, rather than defaulting straight to ZeRO-3 for every project.
9. ZeRO-3 and PEFT Together

blocks.alt: ZeRO-3 combined with PEFT methods produces even greater combined savings

blocks.text: Combining ZeRO-3 with PEFT methods like LoRA, covered in the earlier dedicated module, compounds their savings further, ZeRO-3 handles the sharding of whatever parameters, gradients, and optimizer state exist, while PEFT reduces how many of those parameters are trainable in the first place, together enabling training setups that neither technique alone could achieve.
Worked Example

A team attempting to fine-tune an extremely large model finds that even with ZeRO-2 enabled, the fully replicated model weights alone still exceed their available per-device memory across their cluster of devices.

Moving to ZeRO-3, sharding the model weights themselves in addition to optimizer state and gradients, finally lets the model fit, gathering full weights only temporarily as needed during each layer computation. Combined with LoRA to further reduce their trainable parameter count, they successfully complete a fine-tuning run that would have been completely infeasible under simpler approaches.
Common Mistakes

items: Defaulting to ZeRO-3 for every project without checking whether the lower overhead ZeRO-1 or ZeRO-2 would have sufficed
Underestimating how much communication overhead ZeRO-3 introduces compared to the earlier ZeRO stages
Not considering PEFT methods alongside ZeRO-3 when they could reduce the underlying parameter count needing to be sharded at all
Confusing ZeRO-3's temporary weight gathering with model parallelism's permanent assignment of different model portions to different devices

blocks.text: Practice

For a very large model that does not fit even under ZeRO-2, sketch how combining ZeRO-3 with a PEFT method like LoRA would further reduce the memory burden, addressing both the sharding of existing parameters and the reduction of trainable parameters at once.
Key Takeaway

ZeRO-3 completes the ZeRO progression by sharding model weights in addition to optimizer state and gradients, delivering the maximum memory savings within the ZeRO family at the cost of the highest communication overhead, making it necessary specifically for the largest models while a more conservative ZeRO-1 or ZeRO-2 remains preferable whenever their smaller memory savings are sufficient.
